senses.gloss:
parṇakūrca
(‘[an expiation in which] leaves and dry grass [are used]’)
------------------------------------------
The धर्मशास्त्रस् prescribe expi-ations for a variety of sins—both minor and major—committed by human beings, knowingly or unknowingly. One group of such expiations is given the general name ‘kṛcchara’. The parṇakūrca—also known as ‘parṇakṛcchra’—is one of them.
The sinner for whom this expiation is prescribed, has to give up ड़ोओद् for five days, subsist only on the decoction of boiled leaves (parṇa = leaf) for four days and then, water in which a कूर्च (darbha or Poa cynosuroides) has been dipped.
The recommended leaves are: palāśa (Butea frondosa), udumbara (Ficus glomerata), lotus and बिल्व (Aegle marmelos).
Some works like the Viṣṇudharma-sūtras (46.23) give a longer duration, of seven days, adding the leaves of two more trees.

Parāśarabhaṭṭa
(A. D. 1073-1165)
------------------------------------------
One of the unfinished tasks of यामुनाचार्य (A. D. 912-1042) which Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137) had inherited and promised to fulfil, was the perpetuation of the name of पराशर, the great sage who wrote the Viṣṇupurāṇa. As he was searching for a suitable person to whom he could assign the task, his eyes fell on the young son of his own faithful disciple, कूरेश. He gave him the name ‘Parāśarabhaṭṭa,’ got him trained in the traditional lore of his Vedānta and commanded him to write a detailed commentary on the well-known hymn, the Viṣṇu-sahasranāma (Mahābhārata, Anuśāsanaparva 149). पराशरभट्ट successfully completed his assignment and named his commentary as Bhagavadguṇadarpaṇa (‘a Mirror to the Qualities of the Lord’).
Since he was extremely intelligent and had acquired great scholarship in the श्रीवैष्णव philosophy and traditions, Rāmānuja made him the chief pontiff of the रङ्गनाथ temple complex at श्रीरङ्गम् (in Tamil Nadu).
He had attained mastery in Sanskrit as well as Tamil.
Nine more works—all in Sanskrit—have been attributed to him. Some of them are: Hymns like the Guṇaratnakośa and Śrīraṅgarājastava; Tattvaratnākara; Adhyātmakhaṇḍadvayavivaraṇa and Kriyādīpa.
Vedānta Deśika (A. D. 1268-1369) had been deeply influenced by the writings of पराशरभट्ट.

Parabrahman
(‘Brahman [the Absolute] the Highest’)
------------------------------------------
Treatises of Vedānta describe God, the Absolute, as ‘Brahman’ or ‘Para-ब्रह्मन्’. See BRAHMAN for details.

parāprakṛti
(‘the higher प्रकृति or nature’)
------------------------------------------
Generally most of the Hindu systems of philosophy known as the Ṣaḍdarśanas or the six schools, accept three basic factors as involved in the process of च्रेअतिओन्: the प्रकृति (material matrix); the jīvas (individual souls, unredeemed as yet); and, ईश्वर (God).
Īśvara creates the world out of प्रकृति and involves the jīvas in the bodies made out of that प्रकृति, in accordance with their कर्म or deserts of previous lives.
It is only in the Bhagavadgītā (7.4,5) that we find a classification of प्रकृति as aparā (lower) and parā (higher).
Both these prakṛtis are of the Lord. They belong to him.
The aparāprakṛti is jaḍa (lifeless, non-conscious) and is eightfold: bhūmi (earth); āpas (water); anala (fire); वायु (air); khaṁ (ether or space or sky); मनस् (mind); बुद्धि (intellect); and अहङ्कार (egoity).
The material universe is made out of this.
The जीव (individual सोउल्) is different from this aparāprakṛti and is termed ‘parāprakṛti.’ It is ‘prakṛti’ since it is also involved as a part of च्रेअतिओन्, as a basic factor. It is ‘parā’ or ‘superior’ since it is conscious and is full of life as opposed to the other which is insentient.
The whole universe is a product of these two prakṛtis and ईश्वर, the Lord, is responsible for its evolution or च्रेअतिओन्, sustenance, and involution or destruction.
See also APARĀPRAKṚTI.

parakāyapraveśa
(‘entering into another’s body’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras (3.38) of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) describes parakāya praveśa or ‘entering’ into the body of another person (dead or alive) as one of the yogasiddhis or occult powers gained by a योगि who has succeeded in attaining समाधि (superconscious state).
Every person is imprisoned as it were in the physical body due to the prārabdha-कर्म. A योगि who has attained the सṁयम state (the power of concentration culminating in समाधि) has developed enough power to detach his मिन्द् from his own body and enter into the body of another person—dead or alive—and work through it. This is called परकायप्रवेश.
For this, he should also have a knowledge of the various nāḍīs (tubular structures) through which the prāṇic energy flows or works.
When the योगि thus works through another living person’s body, the latter’s सोउल् or मिन्द् is kept in a temporarily suspended state.
The योगि always uses this power for the good of other people or to exhaust his own प्रारब्धकर्म.
Śaṅkarācārya (A. D. 788-820) is said to have had and used this power once.

paryaṅkaśauca
(‘purification by being seated on a stool’)
------------------------------------------
For one who wants to enter into the fourth stage of life, i.e., सṁन्यास, there is a set procedure. The पर्यङ्कशौच is one in that series of rituals.
Renunciation of the world and entrance into the monastic life are effected through the utterance of the famous praiṣamantra. This is followed by mahāvākyopadeśa or the teaching of the ‘great sentence’ from an Upaniṣad as per the tradition of the गुरु or the teacher.
Then comes the performance of पर्यङ्कशौच. This is actually a ceremonial washing of the saṁnyāsin’s thighs, knees, legs and feet by a householder, after making him sit on a stool. Lumps of clay and water are used in this ceremony.
See also SAṀNYĀSA.

paraśu
(‘[that by which] the enemies are dismembered,’ ‘a battle-axe’)
------------------------------------------
The various deities of the Hindu pantheon are shown not only with many hands but also with several objects including weapons. One such is the परशु (also called khaṇḍaparaśu) or the battle-axe.
It is generally shown in the hands of the male deities like शिव and गणेश, and occasionally in the hands of the देवी also.
Paraśurāma, considered as one of the ten incarnations of विष्णु, had this as his main weapon.

Pārānanda Sūtras
------------------------------------------
The Pārānanda Sūtras also known as the Pārānanda Kalpasūtras, is a work belonging to the तन्त्रस् or शाक्तागमस्. It is a work assigned to the period A. D. 900, though some scholars try to push it back to the period 2400-1800 B. C., perhaps identifying it with the Vedic Kalpasūtra literature.
The work must have been composed at a period when the followers of the tāntrik schools were struggling to get rid of a stigma and endeavouring to be recognised as a part of the Vedic tradition. Hence it is that it declares itself to contain the very cream of the वेदस्.
This treatise—which is prose, in the form of sūtras—is in two adhyāyas or chapters. Each adhyāya is divided into seven āhnikas or subsections. The total number of sūtras is 1585.
Some of the sūtras are short whereas many others are quite long and descriptive.
The work calls God, the Supreme, as परमात्मन्. Under him work seven Īśvaras (lords) of extraordinary powers. They are: ब्रह्मा, विष्णु, शिव, सूर्य, गणेश, शक्ति and भैरव.
Paramātman (God, the Supreme) is the Lord of even the Īśvaras. He is the very embodiment of eternal bliss, life and knowledge. His divinity is supreme and his powers are all-pervading. He is the object of worship of not only the jīvas but also of the Īśvaras.
The next category of sentient beings are the jīvas or individual souls, who are atomic and infinite in number. They are urged to follow the path of धर्म or righteousness and eschew the path of अधर्म or evil which leads them into हेल्ल् with intense suffering.
Three paths of the spiritual disciples are described here: The Dakṣiṇa, the Vāma and the Uttara.
The first one follows the disciplines given in the वेदस्, the smṛtis and the पुराणस्. The second one follows the वेदस् and the तन्त्रस्. The last considers गुरु-vākya, the command of the spiritual preceptor, along with the वेदस्, as very important.
It prescribes a detailed process of दीक्षा or initiation for a disciple by a गुरु who must be a jīvanmukta (liberated सोउल्).
The jīvas aspiring after लिबेरतिओन् are advised to cultivate several virtues like अहिṁसा (non-violence), सत्य (truthfulness), अस्तेय (non-stealing), ब्रह्मचर्य (celibacy), अपरिग्रह (non-acceptance of gifts), स्वाध्याय (study of scriptures), भक्ति (devotion to God), दम (control of senses), mauna (control of speech), शम (peace of मिन्द्), mantrajapa (repetition of the मन्त्र given by the गुरु) and so on.
The work, in addition, deals with the dharmas of the four varṇas and the āśramas as also the four yogas. The efficacies of mantras and mudrās (hand poses), the procedure of observing tāntrik festivals and the use of पञ्चमकारस् (See TANTRAS for details.) also find a place here.

pariṇāmavāda
(‘the theory of change of state’)
------------------------------------------
According to the Brahmasūtras (1.1.2) this world has its origin in ब्रह्मन्, is sustained by It and is dissolved back into It.
Evolution of this world from ब्रह्मन् is explained by the different schools of Vedānta in different ways.
Whereas Advaita Vedānta of शङ्कर (A. D. 788-820) considers this world as a ‘vivarta,’ a mere appearance, Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta of Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137) accepts ‘pariṇaṁa’ or change for ब्रह्मन्. This change may be a change of form like that of clay being shaped into a pot; or of state, like milk becoming curds.
Rāmānuja accepts the latter and hence his view is known as ‘pariṇāma-वाद,’ or ‘Brahmapariṇāmavāda’.

parivrājaka
(‘mendicant’)
------------------------------------------
The institution of सṁन्यास is very old. It is the last of the four āśramas or stations of life.
The word actually means ‘one who roams about all round the place’. A saṁnyāsin was to live by begging and be constantly on the move, never having a fixed abode for himself. This was the discipline imposed on him to cut off all connections of the earlier life and be free to contemplate on God.
See MONASTICISM.

paramapuruṣārtha
(‘the highest [goal of life] aspired after, by a human being’)
------------------------------------------
A पुरुष or a human being is expected to strive for four पुरुषार्थस् or ends in life viz., धर्म (righteousness), अर्थ (wealth), काम (desire for carnal pleasures) and मोक्ष (liberation from transmigratory existence).
Out of these, the last is considered as ‘parama’ or the highest and the best. Hence the name ‘paramapuruṣārtha’.

Parāśara
------------------------------------------
One of the well-known ṛṣis or sages frequently mentioned in the epics and the पुराणस्, पराशर was the son of the sage शक्ति and the grandson of the famous वसिष्ठ.
He is considered as one of the गोत्र-pravartakas or the sages from whom the gotras (patriarchal ancestries) originated.
Learning of the cruel end of his ड़थेर् at the hands of a demon, कल्माषपाद, he started a sacrifice for the destruction of the race of demons.
He was not only a great sage but also a great scholar of the religious lore. His teachings to other sages and kings like जनक contain a lot of information on many abstruse facets of religion and philosophy (vide Mahābhārata, Anuśāsanaparva 146 to 149; 150 to 152).
He was the ड़थेर् of another great sage—Vyāsa or Vedavyāsa—through सत्यवती, the adopted daughter of a chieftain of the fishermen.
Parāśaragītā (Śāntiparva 296-304) and the Parāśarasmṛti are attributed to him.

parikarma
(‘means of refinement’)
------------------------------------------
The Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) is a standard work on Hindu psychology. It deals with the normal मिन्द् and suggests the means and methods of raising it to supernormal levels.
Though it deals with the aṣṭāṅgas or the eight steps as the primary means of controlling the मिन्द् (vide 2.29 to 3.3), it also prescribes seven methods by which the turbulence of the मिन्द् can be controlled and, peace and concentration can be attained. These are called ‘parikarmas’. ‘Parikarma’ means ‘that which refines or purifies’.
These are: cultivating an attitude of friendship towards happy persons, of compassion towards the afflicted, of joy towards the lucky ones and of indifference towards the sinners; प्राणायाम or control of the prāṇic energy through the control of breath; the experience of supernatural smell, taste etc., through certain meditations; seeing a divine light in one’s heart; thinking of the state of मिन्द् of a person who is free from all attachments (i.e., a jīvanmukta); remembering any divine or holy experience got in a dream; meditation on those objects sanctioned or recommended by the scriptures.
By these methods, the turbulence of the मिन्द् can be brought under control.

pāriplava
(‘that which is repeated again and again’)
------------------------------------------
In ancient India, especially for the kings and the emperors, performance of the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् was rather the rule than an exception.
Powerful kings and emperors thought of performing the अश्वमेध sacrifice as a matters of prestige, to establish their supremacy over other rulers.
As a part of this sacrifice, a duly selected horse was let off to roam about as it liked, for a period of one year, after which it would be brought back.
Kings or rulers of the lands where the horse roamed about, were either to accept the sovereignty of the performer of the sacrifice and pay some ransom, or, fight with the army accompanying the horse.
During this one year period, the king who is in yajñadīkṣā (taking vows as per the rules of the sacrifice) has to perform an इष्टि (a simple sacrifice) to Savitṛ (the Sun) three times a day. After the last offering in the evening he has to sit and listen to some ancient legends recited by the होतृ priest (See HOTṚ.) in the presence of other priests. These recitations go by the general name ‘pāriplava’.
A पारिप्लव lasts for ten days. It is repeated 36 times in one year. What exactly should be the legends to be recited on each day is prescribed in the Śrauta-sūtra works. The itihāsas and the पुराणस् are to be recited on the 8th and the 9th nights.
The whole idea seems to be that the मिन्द् of the yajamāna (sacrificer) should be kept on a high plane as much as possible.

pārvaṇasthālīpāka
(‘cooking in a pot on parvan days’)
------------------------------------------
This is one of the minor rites that is classed among the pākayajñas. (See VEDIC SACRIFICES.)
Its name is derived from the fact that it has to be performed on a ‘parvan’ day (a day specified by the holy books as sacred) and ड़ोओद् cooked in a vessel (pāka = cooking; sthālī = vessel) has to be offered into the fire.
A newly married person has to perform this rite after returning home, after मर्रिअगे. It has to be begun on the first full-मोओन् day. The wife has to husk the rice grains and cook it, to prepare it for offering. The husband offers this cooked ड़ोओद् into the fire, first to the deities of the Vedic दर्शपूर्णमास sacrifice and then to अग्नि-Sviṣṭakṛt. The remnants are given to a ब्राह्मण as ड़ोओद्.
Once begun, it has to be performed regularly on the new-मोओन् and the full-मोओन् days throughout life.
The couple has to fast either completely or partially on those days.
It is done both by the आहिताग्नि (one who has kindled the Vedic fires) and the anāhitāgni (one who has not kept the Vedic fires).

paramāṇu
(‘atom’)
------------------------------------------
Generally, all the six systems of Hindu philosophy—known as the Ṣaḍ-darśanas—propound their own theories of च्रेअतिओन् of this world.
The न्याय-Vaiśeṣika systems put forward the theory that the physical world is evolved out of a gradual combination of the paramāṇus of the four basic elements—pṛthvī (earth), ap (water), तेजस् (fire), वायु (air)—and the आकाश (ether) as also the jīvas (individual souls) in accordance with their कर्म, by ईश्वर or God.
When an element like the earth or water is broken into smaller parts, the smallest ultimate particle beyond which further division is impossible, is called ‘paramāṇu’. Only the first four elements can be in the form of paramāṇus or atoms.

Parakāla Maṭha
------------------------------------------
This is one of the prominent maṭhas or monastic centres belonging to the श्रीवैष्णव sect of वैष्णविस्म्.
मठ.jpg" src="http://eoh.rkmathbangalore.org/public/images/thumbs/Parak%C4%81la%20Ma%E1%B9%ADha.jpg" alt="Parakāla मठ at Mysore">Parakāla मठ at MysoreThe original centre was started by Brahmatantra Svatantra Parakāla Svāmin (A. D. 1286-1386), a monastic disciple of वेदान्त देशिक (A. D. 1268-1369), at काञ्चीपुरम् (in Tamil Nadu) in A. D. 1359. It was later on shifted to तिरुपति, मेल्कोटे, श्रीरङ्गपट्टण and finally, to Mysore. The pontiff of this मठ was accepted as the Rājaguru or royal preceptor by Yadurāya, the first king of Mysore.
The presiding deity of this monastery is लक्ष्मी-हयग्रीव. The image of this deity is said to have been given to Rāmānuja (A. D. 1017-1137) by the goddess सरस्वती. The same was handed over by a succession of teachers to वेदान्त देशिक from whom the first pontiff got it.
Till now there has been an unbroken series of pontiffs, the present head—Vāgīśa Brahmatantra Parakālasvāmi—occupying the seat since A. D. 1992.
Though most of them proved to be great teachers, mention may be made of Vāgīśasvāmin (pontificate from A. D. 1915 to 1925) who was endowed with yogic powers and Abhinava रङ्गनाथ Svāmin who was the head for 41 years (from A. D. 1925 to 1966), in whose period there was a tremendous expansion of intellectual activity.

parivedana
(‘obtaining [a wife] leaving [the elder brother]’)
------------------------------------------
The ancient धर्मशास्त्रस् like the Gautama Dharmasūtras (15.18) and the Āpastamba Dharmasūtras (2.5.12.22) declare that a younger brother should not marry before the elder brother. In case he did, he was called ‘parivettā’ and the act itself was known as ‘parivedana’. However, if the elder brother was a lunatic, a patient suffering from an incu-rable serious disease, an impotent person or had become a monk, the younger one was permitted to marry.
This restriction applied to a younger sister also who married before her elder sister. All persons involved in such an act like the parents of the couple and the priest as also the two brothers were considered as sinners who would go to हेल्ल्! Prāyaścittas or expiations were prescribed for them all.
It is rather difficult to understand the लोगिच् behind this prohibition.
This custom seems to have existed among the ancient jews also (vide The Old Testament, Genesis 29).

Parameśvara
(‘the greatest Lord’)
------------------------------------------
Though the word refers to God as the supreme ruler of the universe, it is more commonly used to indicate शिव, the third deity of the Hindu Trinity.
The Viṣṇusahasranāma (name 377) too has used this term for विष्णु.

Pārśvanātha
(circa 800 B. C.)
------------------------------------------
Jainism is one of the oldest religions of the world. It recognises a succession of twenty-four teachers, called ‘Tīrthaṅkaras,’ starting with Vṛṣabhadeva (or ऋषभ-deva) who has been mentioned in the Bhāgavata (5.2 to 6) and other पुराणस्. The last two—considered as historical personalities by the modern historians—are पार्श्वनाथ and वर्धमान महावीर.
Pārśvanātha was the son of Aśvasena (the king of काशी) and Vāmā or Māyādevī.
Refusing to tread the path of worldly life, he started, even as a youth, to travel like a monk all over the country. He taught against हिṁसा or violence of all kinds including those in the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
According to another version, he grew into a great warrior, fought his way up to कलिङ्ग (the modern Orissa), married a princess, the daughter of Prasenajit (the king of कोसल) and lived the life of a householder till the 30th year. Later, the sight of the very picture of Neminātha (the 22nd Tīrthaṅkara) inspired him to renounce the world and roam about as a (Jain) monk.
He taught the principles of जैनिस्म् from his 30th to the 100th year making a very large number of disciples, among whom were kings and noblemen too.
The parents of Vardhamāna Mahā-vīra were also followers of his religion.
Since he is said to have passed away about 250 years before महावीर, he must have lived during the 9th and the 8th centuries B. C. Some scholars opine that he must have lived from 817 B. C. to 717 B. C. or from 838 B. C. to 738 B. C. He passed away in the Pārasnāth Hill, now in North Bihar.
Pārśvanātha taught his followers not to
injure life;
tell lies;
possess any property.
Bhavadevasūri’s Pārśvanāthacarita (A. D. 1356) is the most authoritative work on his life.
In Jain sculpture he is shown with a snake canopy, the snake having 3 or 7 or 9 or 11 hoods. The association with a serpent is rooted in a legend according to which पार्श्वनाथ is said to have saved the life of a huge snake from falling into the fire lit up by a sage Kaṭha who was performing the pañcatapa austerity. (See PAÑCATAPA for details.)
See also JAINISM and VARDAHMĀNA MAHĀVĪRA.

para
(‘the highest’)
------------------------------------------
This word is used in two senses: ‘the other,’ ‘the highest’.
In the latter sense it can be used in all the three genders—masculine, feminine and neuter.
However in the tantras—treatises dealing with the शक्ति or the Divine Mother—it (parā) is used in a technical sense, to indicate the original or the primary state of vāk or speech, the other three states being पश्यन्ती, madhyamā and वैखरी.
In the parā state, speech (or speech energy) is in the potential, unmanifested state. In the पश्यन्ती state, the desire to speak is getting manifested. In the madhyamā, the thought patterns (and sentences) have already evolved. In the वैखरी, the last stage, it is expressed as vocal speech.

Parāśakti
(‘the great शक्ति or power’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism considers God not only as the ड़थेर्, but also as the मोथेर्, of this universe. If God is परब्रह्मन्, he is also पराशक्ति. These two aspects are inseparable even as fire and its burning power are.
According to the शैवागमस्, शिव as the highest Principle differentiates himself—at the time of evolution of this universe—into पराशक्ति (the transcendental, supreme Power), all the while remaining himself unaffected.
From पराशक्ति (Supreme Power) evolves चिच्छक्ति (Power of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्); from Cichhakti comes Ānandaśakti (Power of Bliss); from Ānandaśakti emanates इच्छाशक्ति (Will-power); from इच्छाशक्ति issues ज्ञानशक्ति (Power of Knowledge); and, from this ज्ञानशक्ति emerges क्रियाशक्ति (Power of Action).
Sometimes, the five aspects of शिव like सद्योजात, वामदेव and so on are said to have been derived from the five aspects of शक्ति.
The word पराशक्ति is more frequently used to indicate पार्वती herself.

parivāradevatās
(‘deities surrounding [the main deity]’)
------------------------------------------
In every Hindu temple, in addition to the main deity in the sanctum sanctorum (garbhagṛha), there are other deities surrounding it. They are generally called परिवारदेवतास् and smaller shrines are also built to होउसे them, according to the directions given in the iconographical and architectural works.
These परिवारदेवतास् may be members of the immediate legendary family of the main deity, or other deities associated with it like personal attendants or guar-dians of quarters or commanders of troops and so on.
For instance, in a शिव temple, the following are the परिवारदेवतास्: नन्दि (or Vṛṣabha, the Bull), ब्रह्मा or दुर्गा, सप्तमातृकास् (Seven Mothers like चामुण्डा), गणेश, षण्मुख (Subrah-maṇya), ज्येष्ठा (or अलक्ष्मी), विष्णु and सूर्य.
They are situated respectively in the east, south-east, south, south-west, west, north-west, north and north-east.
The direction in which each of these shrines should face, is also specified.
The Pāṅcarātra texts give a different list of parivāradevatas surrounding the chief deity in a विष्णु temple, such as कपिल, कश्यप, रुद्र, अग्नि, भृगु, सरस्वती, नारद, सूर्य and others.
These deities are situated in the inner round. Other deities may be installed in two outer rounds. Though there is thus a provision for three rounds the last one is rarely executed.

Paraśurāmakalpasūtra
------------------------------------------
This is a digest of Śrīvidyā (See ŚRĪVIDYĀ for details.), a system of Divine मोथेर्’s worship compiled by परशुराम from several sources which were available during his day.
Though in several colophons of the manuscripts, the author is identified with the परशुराम of the epics—son of जमदग्नि and Reṇukā—modern scholars do not agree with the same.
It is a very terse work and can be understood only with the help of the commentary Saubhāgyodaya of Rāmeśvara written during the year A. D. 1831.
The work consists of 328 sūtras spread over 10 khaṇḍas or chapters, each with a different name.
Some scholars feel that this is only the first part and that there is a second part—khanḍas 11 to 18—with 120 sūtras. However, this is not universally conceded.
Though the sūtras are generally short, there are quite a few which are very long.
A brief synopsis of the contents may now be attempted:
Khaṇḍa 1 (Dīkṣāvidhiḥ) (43 sūtras)
Tantras are authoritative scriptures and are not against the वेदस्; only a person of pure मिन्द् is fit to receive this knowledge; upāsanā (meditation) on God generates भक्ति or devotion; practice of tāntrik disciplines is not prohibited in this कलियुग; the 36 principles of तन्त्रस्; some basic information on mantras; on जप and arcanā (ritualistic worship); qualities which a sādhaka should possess; need to have only one गुरु; methods of दीक्षा or initiation; a disciple who receives दीक्षा in one मन्त्र becomes fit for all mantras.
Khaṇḍa 2 (Gaṇanāyakapaddhatiḥ) (10 sūtras)
Method of upāsanā on गणपति and the modes of worship are described here.
Khaṇḍa 3 (Śrīkramaḥ) (23 sūtras)
Etymology of the word ‘Lalitā’; performance of the usual daily rituals; श्रीचक्र and how to draw it; various nyāsas; the two paths viz., Dakṣiṇa and Vāma, or the right-hand path and the left-hand path.
Khaṇḍa 4 (Lalitākramaḥ) (10 sūtras)
Transferring the Paraciti (Supreme चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्, i.e., the goddess शक्ति) into the श्रीचक्र; worship with 64 items; showing nine mudrās; some rituals of worship.
Khaṇḍa 5 (Lalitānavāvaraṇapūjā) (23 sūtras)
Offering pūjās to the nine āvaraṇas or चक्रस् of the श्रीचक्र; other items of पूजा like balidāna (offerings) and pradakṣiṇā (circumambulation).
Khaṇḍa 6 (Śyāmākramaḥ) (39 sūtras)
Meditation on the goddess Śyāmā; method of drawing the Śyāmācakra and its worship; worship of the sandals of the गुरु; worship of a married woman, invoking the goddess in her; जप and other items of पुरश्चरण (See under TANTRAS); rules to be observed by one who does the जप of the मन्त्र of the goddess Śyāmā and of ललिता.
Khaṇḍa 7 (Vārāhīkramaḥ) (38 sūtras)
Obeisance to शिव and the gurus; bījākṣaras of Vārāhīmantra; various nyāsas; worship of Vārāhīcakra or यन्त्र; worship with 16 items; satiating or pleasing the गुरु; पुरश्चरण of the मन्त्र; means of knowing the fulfilment of the repetition of the मन्त्र; on auspicious and inauspicious द्रेअम्स्; rules to be followed while sleeping in the place of doing जप; some details regarding the pañcadaśākṣarīmantra.
Khaṇḍa 8 (Parākramaḥ) (28 sūtras)
Meditation on पराशक्ति (Tripura-sundarī—Lalitā); daily rituals; the special बीज ‘sauḥ’; nyāsas; worship of Sudhādevī; चक्र of Parā; honouring the गुरु; offerings; taking the remaining हविस्.
Khaṇḍa 9 (Homavidhiḥ) (29 sūtras)
Details of the स्थण्डिल (geometrical figure) and the kuṇḍa (sacrificial pit); inscribing the agnicakra; lighting the fire and associated rituals; invoking the deity (iṣṭadevatā) into the fire; details regarding kāmyahoma (desire-motivated होम); होम with the व्याहृतिस् (oṁ bhūḥ etc.); final offering; applying the sacred ash.
Khaṇḍa 10 (Sarvasādhāraṇakramaḥ) (85 sūtras)
This is a general chapter dealing with the various factors which are common to several upāsanās.
Some of them are: Various nyāsas; common factors in a चक्र; bījākṣaras for all mantras; āvāhanamantras; mantras that help in removing obstacles to जप; times suitable for the जप of different mantras; honouring the relatives of the गुरु; obsequial rites; expiatory rites.
The appendix comprising khaṇḍas 11 to 18 deals with some yantras and mantras.

parāvartana
(‘returning [to the original fold]’)
------------------------------------------
Hinduism has never been an aggressive and proselytising type of religion as some Semitic religions are. Over the centuries, many foreign tribes, including those who came as invaders, have been quietly absorbed into the Hindu fold as and when they adopted Hindu ways of life.
However, चोन्वेर्सिओन् from हिन्दुइस्म् to Christianity or Islam has existed for long, as a fact of history, often due to factors other than the voluntary ones. Whenever such converts, an overwhelming majority of whom had been ‘converted’ much against their will, have wished to return to the Hindu fold, there have been several negative factors that have made it difficult for them to return to their मोथेर् religion. These negative factors include the lack of a definite or set procedure for reconversion, and, the hesitation or lack of enthusiasm on the part of the Hindu society to absorb these reconverts. In this again, the caste factor seems to be a great hindrance.
It is interesting, however, to note that later smṛtis like the Devalasmṛti have not only allowed re-entry of such people forcibly converted but also laid some procedures (vide verses 7 to 10 and 53 to 55).
Nevertheless, over the last two centuries serious attempts have been made to popularise the movement of reconversion, generally called ‘śuddhi’. Scholars like P. V. Kāṇe (vide History of धर्म-śāstra, Vol. 4, p. 118, Pune, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, A. D. 1953) and institutions like the Dharmanirṇaya-मण्डल (Lonavala, Maharashtra State) like to call it ‘Parāvartana’ or ‘returning to [the original religion]’.
Attempts have been made to give this process a formal or ritualistic shape. A brief account of one such is described below:
A Śiṣṭasabhā or an assembly of learned persons of pure character should be formed first. The person who wants to return to the Hindu fold should take bath, wear pure white clothes, put a religious mark on the forehead (like sandal paste, विभूति or holy ash and so on) and approach the assembly with his request to re-enter the Hindu fold. The members of the assembly accede, but prescribe certain simple purificatory rites like ड़स्तिन्ग्. They also give him a new set of clothes (suitable for a religious rite or occasion). He performs the purificatory rites and returns again.
The आचार्य, the main leader or teacher who conducts the religious rites, will then make him utter a सङ्कल्प or religious resolve suitable to the occasion. He sits facing the east and makes the new comer to sit on his right side.
This is followed by a regular होम (offering oblations into a duly consecrated fire) with Vedic mantras. At the end, the newcomer too participates directly in the होम by way of purification. He is also given a new name. Then he accepts the gift of a new copy of the sacred book, the Bhagavadgītā, and is made to chant certain parts of it (like the 16th chapter, verses 1 to 3). He is advised to try to cultivate the virtues mentioned there.
The participants are given the prasāda (consecrated ड़ोओद्), after which all will disperse.
(For details of the whole procedure, vide: P. V. Kane, History of Dharmaśāstra Vol. 4, pp. 828-830, Pune, Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, A. D. 1953.)
See also CONVERSION.

Pārvaṇaśrāddha
------------------------------------------
This is one of the several śrāddhas performed to appease the departed souls. It is more common and still in use.
See ŚRĀDDHA for details.

Paryāyamahotsava
(‘celebration [of taking over the temple] by turns’)
------------------------------------------
See UḌUPI.

pariṇāminitya
(‘an [entity which] is real, [but] changing’)
------------------------------------------
This is a basic concept of the Sāṅkhya philosophy.
The उपनिषद्स् accept the आत्मन्/ ब्रह्मन् as immutable and as the only reality. The world is said to be a च्रेअतिओन् from or out of It. Sāṅkhya philosophy considers this as self-contradictory, since what is real and immutable cannot undergo any change.
Hence it accepts two basic realities—the पुरुष or the conscious self, and, the प्रकृति or the insentient matrix of all matters.
The latter, though real, is not immutable. It changes or evolves into this world. Hence it is called ‘pariṇāminitya’.

Pārvatī
(‘daughter of the mountain-king’)
------------------------------------------
Pārvatī is the power and consort of शिव, the god of disintegration and destruction. An overwhelming majority of the goddesses of हिन्दुइस्म् are aspects and variations of पार्वती. The names by which she is known or worshipped are too numerous to mention. If some of the names like पार्वती, हैमवती, Girijā and दाक्षायणी indicate her origin from the हिमालयस् or दक्ष (one of the forefathers of mankind), other names like Śivā, Mṛḍānī, Rudrāṇī and Śarvāṇi stress her aspect as the spouse of शिव. Still others like Aparṇā and Umā have specific reference to certain stories in the paurāṇic literature.
One of the earliest references to this deity is found in the Kenopaniṣad (3.12) where she is mentioned as ‘Umā Haima-vatī’ enlightening इन्द्र, the king of gods, about ब्रह्मन्, the Absolute or God. This reference is enough to conclude that the worship of this goddess is very ancient.
According to the paurāṇic accounts, in her ‘first’ इन्चर्नतिओन्, she was Dākṣā-yaṇī, the daughter of दक्ष and Prasūti, and married to Lord शिव. Unable to understand Lord शिव’s greatness, दक्ष once reviled him and started harbouring hatred towards him. When दक्ष undertook the performance of a great sacrifice, the notable exception among the dignitaries invited was शिव himself. Much against the advice of her spouse, दाक्षायणी went to the sacrifice uninvited and being slighted, ended her life by igniting herself through the fire of योग. Hence she came to be known as सती, the chaste one. She was next reborn as पार्वती, the daughter of Himavān and Menā. After performing intense austerities she succeeded in pleasing शिव and making him accept her again as his consort.
During the performance of these severe austerities, she refused to eat even dry leaves to sustain herself and hence got the appellation Aparṇā. Her मोथेर् Menā unable to see her dear daughter languishing by austerities, tried to dissuade her by the words, ‘U mā’ (= my dear, don’t do like this!) which became her another name (Umā). Being the daughter of the हिमालयस् (the abode of snow) she has to be गौरी (the white one). As the मोथेर् of the universe she is अम्बा and अम्बिका, both the words meaning ‘mother’.
Like her consort शिव, she also has two aspects: the mild and the terrible. As पार्वती or Umā she represents the mild aspect. In this aspect she is usually shown with शिव. Then she has only two hands, the right hand holding a blue lotus and the left hanging loosely by the side. The image is richly decorated. When represented independently she is shown with four hands, two hands holding red and blue lotuses and the other two exhibiting the varada and abhaya mudrās.
Though all the female deities are called Śaktis of their male counterparts, the words ‘Śakti’ and ‘Devī’ are more particularly—or even exclusively—used to denote the शक्ति of शिव, the innumerable aspects of पार्वती. Considering शिव as महादेव, the Supreme God, पार्वती represents his power by which the universe is created, sustained and destroyed.
The हिमालयस् represent the आकाश or ether, the first fundamental substance. Menā stands for intelligence. Hence पार्वती, their offspring, represents the conscious substance of the universe. That is why she is also called Umā (= light, the bright one).
At the subjective level, Umā-Haima-vatī represents ब्रह्मविद्या or spiritual wisdom, by which union with शिव or God is attained.
Being the consort of शिव, who is रुद्र, the terrible, she also has her terrible aspects which need a separate study.
It is interesting to note that the Vaiṣṇava symbols—Śaṅkha and Cakra—are often shown in her hands also. Though the पुराणस् describe her as the sister of विष्णु, it is possible that विष्णु is consi-dered as the active power of शिव and hence these symbols in the hands of the देवी. This surmise is strengthened by the fact that in the Haryardhamūrti of शिव, the left half is विष्णु and in the अर्ध-नारीश्वर form, देवी forms the left half.

Paraśurāma
(‘Rāma of the battle-axe’)
------------------------------------------
Paraśurāma has been listed as the sixth अवतार or इन्चर्नतिओन् of विष्णु among the ten, commonly known as दशावतारस्.
Since राम (or श्रीराम) was his contemporary and drew his power into himself, परशुराम is often considered as a partial or temporary manifestation of the Lord विष्णु.
Paraśurāma was the son of the great sage जमदग्नि and रेणुका (daughter of the king Prasenajit).
Once, he was commanded by his ड़थेर् to cut off the head of his मोथेर् which he did. However, by praying to his ड़थेर्, he got her restored to life.
During his absence, कार्तवीर्यार्जुन, the king of माहिष्मती, visited the hermitage of जमदग्नि who entertained him in a royal way. This was due to the power and grace of Kapilā, the wish-yielding divine cow. When the king wanted it for himself and the sage refused to part with it, he killed the sage and ransacked the whole place.
Learning, after his return, of what had happened, परशुराम did severe penance to please Lord शिव and obtained a divine परशु or battle-axe from him. With this he killed, not only Kārtavīryār-juna but also many other क्षत्त्रिय kings who had become tyrants and were terrorising their subjects.
However, in his encounter with राम, he lost all his power and went away for तपस् to the महेन्द्र mountains.
He is said to be a cirajīvin (an immortal) and hence, still living.
He was a great warrior and an expert in the use of various weapons. द्रोणाचार्य and कर्ण were his disciples.
Once, he had to fight with भीष्म, the grandsire, but could not vanquish him.
Though he advised दुर्योधन to make peace with the Pāṇḍavas, Duryo-dhana refused to heed it.
Some Vaiṣṇavāgamas like the Ahirbudhnya Saṁhitā and their commentaries like the Tattvatraya consider him as a secondary aspect (svarūpāveśa) of विष्णु.
Iconographical works picture him as a sage, red-complexioned with white robes and जटामुकुट (crown of hair). He holds the परशु in his right hand and the vaiṣṇavadhanus (bow of विष्णु) in the left. The left hand may also be in the tarjanī-मुद्रा or pose of warning or threat.
In some rare cases he may be shown with four hands like विष्णु.
His jayantī (birthday) falls on the Akṣayatṛtīyā day (generally in May).

pariṣad
(‘a gathering of people sitting around’)
------------------------------------------
Though the वेदस् and allied literature give general rules and guidance about धर्म, they do not offer solutions to all the problems that arise in the life of an individual or society. Hence, the ancient sages advised a person in doubt about a particular mode of conduct, to consult or observe the wise ब्राह्मणस् (vide Taittirīya Upaniṣad 1.11).
In course of time ‘pariṣads’ of learned men—known earlier as ‘sabhās’ or ‘samitis’—were recommended for deciding such issues concerning धर्म and even pres-cribing expiations for transgressions.
A परिषद् should consist of at least ten śiṣṭas (good and great men of character) though it could be less, if such men are not available in the required number. However, a परिषद् of only one person—though permitted theoretically under extraordinary circumstances—was not encouraged.
The members of the pariṣads were to be experts in the Vedic lore as also the धर्मशास्त्रस् and vyavahāra (social conduct). They were to be persons of exceptional character and merit. They must be competent to decide the subtlest points of धर्म and offer the necessary solutions and guidance when the problems were brought before them. They should also be capable of prescribing the necessary expiations for sins depending on their gravity.
Generally, the king of the land as also a monk of exceptional merit were part of the परिषद्. Though the king might not sit with the members of the परिषद्, his consent to the decisions taken was compulsory. However, even the king could not take any decision in such matters without consulting the परिषद्.

paryagnikaraṇa
(‘moving the firebrand round [the melted butter]’)
------------------------------------------
Ājya or ghee is an important material used in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्. After it is kept in the vessel known as ājyasthālī, it has to be ceremonially purified before being offered into the consecrated fire. This is done by moving an ulmuka or a firebrand three times round the आज्य contained in that vessel, placed over the fire. This particular act is called ‘paryagnikaraṇa’. The whole procedure is known as ‘ājyasaṁskāra’. The आज्य is said to acquire a special lustre by this purificatory process.
The fire for the firebrand is drawn from the आहवनीय fire.
The other objects for पर्यग्निकरण are: यूप (sacrificial post), आहवनीय fire itself, cātvāla (a pit) and śāmitra (a minor fire used in वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्).

Pārijāta
(‘that which was born on the other shore’)
------------------------------------------
The कल्पतरु or the wish-yielding tree is said to have been born out of the ocean during समुद्रमथन or the churning of the ocean for obtaining the अमृत or ambrosia. (See SAMUDRAMATHANA for details.)
According to other versions found in the पुराणस्, the कल्पतरु is not one tree but a general name indicating five such trees, all of them having the same powers of fulfilling the wishes of those that seek them. These trees situated in इन्द्र’s garden in हेअवेन् are: Haricandana, कल्प-vṛkṣa, Mandāra, पारिजात (or Pārijātaka) and Santāna.
Once अदिति, the first wife of the great sage कश्यप, pleased him by her devoted service. When he asked her to seek a boon she wished to possess quite a few things, to get even one of which, it was so difficult! However, कश्यप created the पारिजात tree which had the power to grant anything that its possessor would ask for.
Since कश्यप created it in a place on the opposite bank of the river गङ्गा, it was called ‘Pāri-jāta’ (‘born on the other shore’).
Once, Śrīkṛṣna, at the request of queen सत्यभामा, is said to have uprooted it from इन्द्र’s garden and planted it in his own royal garden in द्वारका.

Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtras
------------------------------------------
The गृह्यसूत्रस् are one of the earliest phases of the dharmaśāstra literature.
The Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtras is a well-known work, assigned to the Śukla Yajurveda tradition and followed mostly in North India.
Nothing is known about the sage Pāraskara except that he was a disciple of the sage कात्यायन who was the author of the Śrautasūtras bearing his name. According to one view, Pāraskara might have lived during the period 900-800 B. C. However it is difficult to prove it conclusively.
The work is in three kāṇḍas or chapters.
The following table gives an idea of the work:
Kāṇḍa (Chapter) Kaṇḍikās(Subsections) Sūtras
First 19 197
Second 17 294
Third 16 219
Total : 3 52 710

The topics dealt with are, briefly, as follows:
On वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् in general; the saṁskāra or the sacrament of विवाह or मर्रिअगे; दर्शपूर्णमास and Vaiśva-deva sacrifices; some more सṁस्कारस् generally included in the group of sixteen (= ṣoḍaśasaṁskāras); on eating flesh; उपनयन and the duties of ब्रह्मचारिन्; a special sacrifice called Sītāyajña to be performed in the spring season; the sacrifice called Āgrayaṇī to be performed with the newly harvested crop; some miscellaneous subjects like a cure for headaches, controlling one’s employees, a few prāyaścittas or expiations for sins, modes of getting into a chariot and entering an assembly where many people have gathered.
Five commentaries on this Gṛhya-sūtras have been discovered: by Gadādhara; by हरिहर (Hariharabhāṣya) by Karkācārya; by Jayarāma; and by Viśvanātha. There is one gloss called Amṛtavyākhyā, quoted by other writers, but the author is not known.

parā-vidyā
(‘the highest knowledge’)
------------------------------------------
See APARĀ-VIDYĀ.

parisaṅkhyāvidhi
(‘exclusive injunction’)
------------------------------------------
The पूर्वमीमाṁसा system describes three kinds of vidhis or Vedic injunctions. They are: apūrvavidhi, नियमविधि and परिसङ्ख्याविधि. (See विधि">APŪRVAVIDHI and NIYAMAVIDHI.)
These vidhis or injunctions are helpful in ascertaining the correct meaning of the Vedic sentences, especially with regard to the performance of sacrifices.
When a general rule seems to apply equally to two alternatives and only one has to be allowed, precluding the other, the विधि or injunction that prescribes it is called ‘parisaṅkhyāvidhi’.
‘Pari’ means varjana or excluding. ‘Saṅkhyā’ means knowledge. Hence the परिसङ्ख्याविधि gives us the knowledge of what is to be avoided in a particular situation.
For instance: A cart, to which a horse and a mule are yoked, is taken out to bring the clay necessary for preparing bricks (for the altar of a sacrifice). At a certain stage of the journey, the person driving the cart has to ‘recite a Vedic मन्त्र holding the rein.’ Since both the animals have reins, the doubt arises as to which one should be held. The Vedic मन्त्र states clearly that the rein of the horse is to be held. Hence, the other—the rein of the mule—is to be excluded. Therefore this injunction becomes a ‘pari-saṅkhyāvidhi’.
Writers on the Mīmāṁsā point out three defects in this विधि, but they are not of much consequence.

pariśiṣṭa
(‘supplement’)
------------------------------------------
The word परिशिष्ट means ‘what is left over, unsaid’. Though the कल्पसूत्रस्, the last of the वेदाङ्गस्, deal with वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस् also, they often do not give all the details necessary. Perhaps, during the period of their composition, quite a few things had been taken for granted. However, when in course of time, these details were being forgotten, it became necessary to put them in writing for the guidance of the future generations. This gave rise to pariśiṣṭas, anukramaṇīs and चरण-व्यूहस्.
The परिशिष्ट works are generally in the form of ślokas in the anuṣṭubh metre. They deal with many details connected with the वेदिच् सच्रिड़िचेस्.
The Āśvalāyana-gṛhya-pariśiṣṭa which has four chapters, deals with subjects related to the Ṛgveda.
The Gobhilasaṅgraha-pariśiṣṭa belongs to the Sāmaveda. It deals with gṛhyakarmas or rites to be performed in one’s home, as also some kāmyakarmas or desire-motivated actions.
Karmapradīpa is another परिशिष्ट work attributed to either गोभिल or कात्यायन. It is known by other names also such as Sāmagṛhya, Chandogapariśiṣṭa and Gobhilasmṛti.
The Nigamapariśiṣṭa and the Pravarādhyāya of कात्यायन are assigned to the Śukla Yajurveda tradition.
See also ANUKRAMAṆĪ and CARAṆA-VYŪHA.

Parāśara Smṛti
------------------------------------------
If the वेदस् and the उपनिषद्स् give the basic philosophy of हिन्दुइस्म्, the धर्मशास्त्रस्, comprising the smṛtis, the पुराणस् and the निबन्धस् (digests), give the rules and regulations that guide a Hindu in his personal and social life.
One of the more ancient smṛtis extant even now, is the Parāśara Smṛti. It has twelve chapters and 602—or 592 according to its own statement at the end—verses.
The following is a brief summary of its contents.
Chapter 1 (65 verses)
Knowledge of धर्म; on the four युगस्; six daily duties like bath, सन्ध्या ritual and Vedic studies; proper means of livelihood for the three lower varṇas.
Chapter 2 (20 verses)
Duties of a householder.
Chapter 3 (55 verses)
Aśauca (ceremonial impurity) and purificatory processes.
Chapter 4 (34 verses)
On सुइचिदे; punishment for a wife who deserts her husband; remarriage of women under certain conditions; in praise of chaste widows.
Chapter 5 (24 verses)
Minor expiations.
Chapter 6 (75 verses)
Expiations for prāṇihatyā (killing animals and human beings).
Chapter 7 (44 verses)
Purification of various articles such as vessels of wood and metal; about women in menses.
Chapter 8 (50 verses)
Expiations for the killing of cows and oxen unwillingly; constitution of a परिषद् (assembly) of ब्राह्मणस्.
Chapter 9 (60 verses)
Taking proper care of one’s cows.
Chapter 10 (43 verses)
Certain expiations like चान्द्रायण and सान्तपन.
Chapter 11 (55 verses)
Expiations for the violation of the rules regarding the partaking of ड़ोओद्; purification of wells polluted by animals.
Chapter 12 (77 verses)
On various kinds of bath; bath for purification; expiations for mortal sins like murder of a ब्राह्मण, consuming liquor, stealing of gold and so on.
This स्मृति contains several views considered as peculiar, like eulogising the practice of सती (self-immolation by a widow on the funeral pyre of her husband).
Numerous verses in it also occur in other स्मृति-works like those of मनु and बौधायन.
Later writers of निबन्धस् quote पराशर frequently.
Mādhavācārya (= विद्यारण्य) (14th cent. A. D.) has written a voluminous commentary called Parāśaramādhavīya on this स्मृति.
See also BṚHATPARĀŚARASAṀHITĀ.

Paramātman
(‘the Supreme Self’)
------------------------------------------
If each of the individual souls is called ‘jīvātman’, God is called Paramāt-man as opposed to him. परमात्मन् is the same as ब्रह्मन्.
See BRAHMAN for more details.

pāramārthika
(‘relating to the highest truth’)
------------------------------------------
Truth (‘sattā’) according to Advaita metaphysics is of three types: प्रातिभासिक (apparent), vyāvahārika (practical) and पारमार्थिक (the highest).
When we wrongly perceive the upright ears of a hare as its horns, it is ‘prātibhāsika’ sattā. This world of senses is ‘vyāvahārika’ sattā since it is real for all practical purposes. ब्रह्मन् or God which is the highest and unchanging truth is ‘pāramārthika’ sattā.

pariṇāma
(‘change’)
------------------------------------------
According to the साङ्ख्य-योग systems of इन्दिअन् फिलोसोफ्य्, any object can undergo two types of ‘pariṇāma’ or change. (This is sometimes called ‘vikāra’ also.) The first concerns the change of form and name, but not of the substance itself. For instance, when gold is converted into ornaments it changes only in form and name. The substance gold continues to remain the same. So is the case with a jar made of clay. The second concerns the change in the substance itself, as for instance, when milk becomes curds.
Sometimes the pariṇāmas are classified as three, from another standpoint: धर्म-परिणाम, लक्षण-परिणाम and अवस्था-परिणाम.
When an object like clay loses its lump form which is a ‘dharma’ (characteristic) for it and takes the form of a pot, the change is termed as ‘dharma-परिणाम’ (change of form or characteristic).
The word ‘lakṣaṇa’ is a technical term and means change of time. When the same change, i.e., the clay of the past becoming the pot of the present, is looked at from the standpoint of time, it is called ‘lakṣaṇa-परिणाम’ (change in time). The same pot is ‘new’ now, but becomes ‘old’ after sometime. This change of state is called अवस्था-परिणाम.
Two more ‘pariṇāmas’ are mentioned in the Sāṅkhya works. When प्रधान, the matrix of all inanimate objects of this world, is in a state of equilibrium (before च्रेअतिओन्), each of its three guṇas viz., सत्त्व, रजस् and तमस्, is undergoing only internal change without interfering with the other two guṇas. Such a change is called ‘svarūpa-परिणाम’ or ‘change into the homogeneous’. When the guṇas start affecting one another, each getting the upper hand by turns, then, the change is called ‘virūpa-परिणाम’ or ‘change into the heterogeneous’.

paramahaṁsa
(‘the great swan’)
------------------------------------------
Some of the पुराणस् as also the धर्मशास्त्रस् categorise the saṁnyāsins (Hindu मोन्क्स्) into four groups: the kuṭīcakas, the bahūdakas, the haṁsas and the paramahaṁsas.
A कुटीचक (‘one who lives in a hut’) is one who lives in an आश्रम (monastery), eats only eight morsels of ड़ोओद् per day and performs yogic practices.
A बहूदक (‘one who drinks water from many sources’) wears the ochre-coloured cloth (an insignia of a Hindu monk) and carries a कमण्डलु (water-pot prepared out of the bitter gourd) as also a tridaṇḍa (staff made of three bamboo sticks tied together). He lives by begging from not more than seven houses.
The हṁस (‘the swan’) is an ekadaṇḍi (has one staff only, signifying the control of the मिन्द्), lives under trees or in mountain caves and such other solitary places, going into the village once a day for begging his ड़ोओद्.
The परमहṁस (‘the great swan’) is the best of these four saṁnyāsins. He is said to live in deserted places, च्रेमतिओन् grounds or dilapidated structures. He is completely indifferent to physical comforts and is perfectly equanimous under all circumstances of life.
The word ‘paramahaṁsa’ itself perhaps means a person possessing supreme discrimination (like a हṁस or a swan which can leave off water and drink only milk from the diluted mixture of the two) which ultimately results in the knowledge of ब्रह्मन्. Or, it may also mean a person of the highest spiritual experience, who is constantly aware that he is one with ब्रह्मन् (ham = aham = I; saḥ = he, God or ब्रह्मन्).
Works like the Vaikhānasa Sūtras (8.9), Laghuviṣṇupurāṇa (4.14.23), Bhikṣu-kopaniṣad and Sūtasaṁhitā (Mānayoga-khaṇḍa 6) give a description of these four types of saṁnyāsins.

Parīkṣit
------------------------------------------
Parīkṣit was the son of prince अभिमन्यु and उत्तरा (the daughter of the king विराट), and grandson of अर्जुन and सुभद्रा.
After the महाभारत war, Aśvat-thāma the vengeance-incarnate, discharged the ब्रह्मास्त्र towards the womb of उत्तरा who was pregnant, to destroy the entire race of the Pāṇḍavas. परीक्षित्, the baby in the womb died and was stillborn. However, Lord कृष्ण, revived the baby by his divine powers.
It is said that the Lord विष्णु had given him his vision and the baby-boy started examining every nook and corner through his eyes, to find the Lord. Hence he came to be known as परीक्षित् (= ‘one who examines or searches’).
The Pāṇḍavas crowned him as the king and left on their final journey (‘mahāprasthāna’).
His queen was Bhadravatī—also known as Irāvatī—in whom he had four sons: जनमेजय, Śrutasena, Ugrasena and Bhīmasena.
After being crowned as the king, he drove away Kalipuruṣa—the personification of evil of the age of Kali—and ruled the kingdom righteously for sixty years.
Once, as ill-luck would have it, he showed disrespect to Śamīka, a great sage, who was in deep-meditation, by ‘garlanding’ him with a dead snake. Being cursed by Śṛṅgī (Śamīka’s son) to die of snake bite within a week, he ultimately died of the same, the snake being तक्षक himself (the king of snakes).
It was during his last seven days that he listened to the recitation of the Bhāgavata by the sage शुक.
See also ĀSTIKA and JANAMEJAYA.

Parāśaragītā
------------------------------------------
The epics and the पुराणस् contain several religious discourses that go by the name ‘Gītā,’ in imitation of the famous Bhagavadgītā. One such, from the epic, the Mahābhārata, is the Parāśaragītā. It forms a part of the Śāntiparva (chapters 290 to 298). It has nine chapters, the total number of verses being 288. The sage पराशर is the teacher while the king जनक is the recipient of the teaching.
A brief summary of the same may now be given:
Chapter 1 (26 verses)
Dharma is the best means of obtaining श्रेयस् or spiritual welfare. Karmas give their results, good or bad. Cultivation of virtues like दम (self control), kṣamā (forgiveness), सत्य (truth) leads to happi-ness. People ruin themselves by going against their स्वधर्म (duties allotted to them).
Chapter 2 (23 verses)
Since a human birth and a long life are difficult to obtain, one should do only good actions and avoid bad actions. The law of कर्म is inexorable. Sins committed out of इग्नोरन्चे can be erased through proper expiations but not the ones committed intentionally.
Chapter 3 (23 verses)
Money earned through धर्म, the righteous means, is good. Serving guests is a pious act.
Everyone is born under certain ṛṇas or debts like देव-ऋण and ṛṣi-ṛṇa, debts towards gods and sages, and should discharge oneself from them as described in the holy scriptures.
Prayer to God and performance of good actions are of great help in life.
Chapter 4 (21 verses)
Eulogy of the benefits wrought by the company of holy men is stressed here. So also, the importance of following the dharmas (duties) that accrue to one as per his वर्ण and आश्रम, is highlighted.
Chapter 5 (31 verses)
This chapter describes as to how the people of the four varṇas should live. They should abandon all forbidden actions.
When the āsurī or demoniac tendencies rose in the hearts of human beings making them inclined towards evil, Lord शिव destroyed them. The decimation of the Tripuras (the three cities of the demons and the demons themselves) by Lord शिव is symbolic of this.
Chapter 6 (39 verses)
A person deeply attached to sense-pleasures gradually goes down whereas the one who performs his duties properly and also तपस् or austerities, raises himself and attains perfection in course of time. This is the gist of the teachings of this chapter.
Chapter 7 (39 verses)
While continuing the topic of the varṇas, पराशर declares here that a person born in a higher वर्ण, automatically goes down to the lower ones if he neglects his duties. On the other hand, persons of lower varṇas can raise themselves to higher levels through तपस्.
Chapter 8 (40 verses)
This chapter deals with the following subjects: importance of sweet speech; various kinds of death; some rules regarding wars and battles; realisation of the आत्मन् puts an end to transmigration; greatness of a person, who being born as a human being, attains आत्मज्ञान or realisation; auspiciousness of dying in the उत्तरायण (northern solstice); need for serving the spiritually great ones; condemnation of सुइचिदे; eulogy of performing good deeds as also giving gifts and bathing in sacred rivers.
Chapter 9 (46 verses)
Importance of asaṅgatva (non-attachment) and a beautiful description of a man who has attained that state is the main topic of this concluding chapter.
This short work is definitely a useful addition to the गीता-literature.
